title: Rey's Perfect Paper Boat Parade
markdown:
Young Rey, who kept an eye on the sky for the village, had a brand-new idea one blustery afternoon. Not about clouds. About the brook that giggled toward Nana Tess’s prize petunias.

“A paper boat parade!” Already folding faster than a hummingbird’s wings. Saffron, Rey’s parrot, a magnificent splash of rainbow feathers, puffed his chest. “Parade! Parade! Rey’s parade!”

Rey launched the first boat, a neat little tug. Splish, splash. It bobbed, a tiny white explorer. Then gurgle, gulp — a big drink, down like a soggy sock. “Oh no!” Saffron shrieked, “Sank! Sank! Soggy boat!” Rey folded a wider one. It wiggled and jiggled, then surrendered to the stream. Shoulders drooped. A sinking disaster. “No use.” A puff of frustration.

Nana Tess appeared, smile as bright as spring daffodils. “What’s all this gloom?” Soft as a favourite blanket. Rey pointed at the wet paper bits. “They keep sinking. Not a parade. A swim lesson.”

She knelt. “A puzzle. What if we change just one thing at a time, and see?”

Rey looked puzzled. “One change? I want them to be the best.” Saffron tilted his head. “One change! Smart, smart!”

Tess picked up fresh paper. “Like your first one. Identical.” Quick creases. “Now — one tiny pebble in the bottom.” They launched it. Whoosh. It did not just sink; it zipped like a tiny submarine and vanished. “Adding that pebble made it sink quicker. That tells us something.”

Rey’s eyes widened. A puzzle with rules. “If a pebble makes it sink faster — what if we don’t add one? What if the sail on another boat is smaller?” Rey folded again, main sail creased flat so it would catch less wind. A hopeful flick. Whoosh. Glide. The little boat danced and, with a final curve, reached the edge of Tess’s bright pond. Saffron flapped. “Hooray!”

Rey buzzed. “Lighter. Smaller sails.” A happy flurry: rustling paper, quick folds, excited squawks. One boat had a bit of weight taken from its base. Another had its sail trimmed. One hull more pointed, like an arrowhead. Each launch a lesson — every wobble, every glide written in the water for a moment.

Finally, a fleet. Rey held them up. “We changed only one thing at a time.” A cheer. Whoosh, whoosh, whoosh. The boats sailed, bobbing, sails catching the breeze just right, one after another into the pond. A proper parade.

Tess watched, proud, and named the method once: a fair test. Each small change visible. She did not ask what else they could try. Rey felt the warm swell anyway. Saffron ruffled and, because he was Saffron, still squawked “Best parade ever!” which was allowed, being a parrot and not a sermon. Rey stacked the leftover paper under a stone so the wind, which had started the afternoon, could not start a second experiment without them.
